MarketWatch: Almost double the amount of large-capitalization U.S. stocks moved in the opposite direction to the wider market this year than during the peak of the dot-com crash, according to an asset management firm.

According to quant strategist Kyle Schmidt of NISA Investment Advisers, 27% of large U.S. stocks had negative realized beta in the six months ended Sept. 30, versus a long-run average of 1.3% and a rate of 14% in 2020, when technology stocks crashed.

That's the highest since at least 1990. "This dislocation is extreme in both breadth and duration and has significant implications for portfolio and risk management," Schmidt said.

"We see the market as clearly splitting along the dimension of AI and most everything else," he added.

Per FactSet’s John Butters, the Mag 7 are now reporting lower Q3 earnings growth than the other 493: 22.6% vs. 32.6%. If that holds through the end of earnings season, it’s the first time since Q4 2022. On Sep 30 the expectation was the reverse, at 33.6% vs. 27.8%.

But note it’s largely a function of big GAAP charges at two companies (FactSet uses GAAP EPS for Alphabet, Amazon and Meta):
▪ Meta: −41% vs. estimate, with a $9.89B litigation charge in the quarter
▪ Alphabet: −30% vs. estimate, with $8.7B of net losses on equity securities
▪ Amazon: a tough comparison, since year-ago EPS included $9.5B in pre-tax gains on its Anthropic stake

Microsoft and Tesla both beat, and Apple reports next week while NVIDIA doesn’t report until Nov 17.

The part that isn’t accounting: analysts also expect the Mag 7 to trail in Q4 (22.6% vs. 30.8%), and that gap has widened since Sep 30 (23.6% vs. 28.3%). 

The 493 are being lifted by Energy, where Q4 estimates rose 20.3% in October.

Richmond Fed President Barkin (not an #FOMC voter this year but will be in 2027), in a SiriusXM interview Friday (link below) agrees with fellow regional Fed presidents Logan and Musalem that “the direction of travel is pretty straightforward — the question, though, is pace,” adding “[a] gradual approach is a good way to go, and we’ll see what we learn over the next period of time.”

“Gradual makes sense when you’re not much behind the curve, where you want time to learn both from the economic environment and the external environment.”

What’s driving his view is demand. He said consumer spending has been surprisingly resilient given relatively flat incomes, and demand is solid outside of nonprofits and housing. Businesses tell him cost pressures are broad-based, and after years of elevated inflation they’re planning to pass those costs on.

Barkin said the AI investment surge is straining supply chains, and that “kind of demand-side inflation, that’s not a supply-side shortage issue,” unlike the energy price shock from the Iran war.

“We’ll see how long that pressure lasts. But if we do see a continued surge in demand, that would be the kind of thing you might want to lean against.”

Notably that comes after equipment spending added 1.16 points to Q3 GDP, the most since Q3 2011 outside of Q3 2020. Of that computers and peripheral equipment added 0.72 point, the largest contribution on record in data back to 1959.

H/t to @C_Barraud, who flagged ahead of the euro area GDP release that he was looking for a GDP beat. And beat it did: GDP grew 0.4% in the third quarter, double the 0.2% Bloomberg consensus (prior 0.6%), and 1.3% year-over-year versus 1.1% expected, per Reuters.

The headline flatters, though. Bloomberg Economics estimates Ireland (+5.5%, driven again by multinationals) accounted for about half the increase, with the four largest economies averaging just 0.1%:

▪️ Spain +0.6%
▪️ Netherlands +0.6%
▪️ Germany +0.2%
▪️ Italy 0.0%
▪️ France -0.1%

But it's France which is the real problem here. The contraction missed the 0.1% consensus and was its second this year (-0.2% in the first quarter, flat in the second), so the French economy has not grown at all in 2026. Investment fell 0.6%, and net exports subtracted 0.6 percentage points, more than offsetting a 0.4% gain in household consumption, per Insee.

That’s a real problem for France’s debt math. Public debt hit 119.0% of GDP at the end of the second quarter, up from 115.6% a year earlier (Insee), with the deficit running at 5.4% of GDP. The government’s 0.5% growth forecast for 2026 is now out of reach (Insee puts the carryover at just 0.2%), which makes its 5.0% deficit target for 2027 that much harder to hit, assuming the budget even gets through parliament.

Meanwhile, the 10-year OAT sits near 4.9%, roughly 155 to 160 basis points over Bunds, near the widest since the 2011-12 euro crisis. With zero real growth and marginal borrowing costs that high, the interest bill is projected to climb to about €91 billion in 2027 from about €79 billion this year. 

Stagnation shrinks the tax base a recovery depends on, and with the ECB eyeing a third hike in December and in the midst of a leadership change and French presidential elections in 2027 where the far right leads polls, relief isn’t likely coming from Frankfurt or Paris anytime soon.

Dallas Fed President Logan (an #FOMC voter this year), who dissented in favor of a hike in July, but, a little surprisingly given her hawkish bent, went along with this week’s hold, in remarks to Davidson College students today (link below) made clear the skip changes the timing, not the destination, saying the FOMC “needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases. After that, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate."

She explains why she was fine skipping October: “Financial markets have been volatile in response to news on the technology investment outlook and geopolitical developments. In such an environment, adjusting policy more gradually can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary. Moreover, as long as market participants understand the FOMC’s policy plans, the precise timing of each rate increase has little effect on the longer-term rates most borrowers pay.”

“Indeed, by making the destination clear, the FOMC can better help the economy adapt and obtain the promised benefits of a skip.”

On inflation, she notes “While inflation has come down from the post-pandemic peak, it is not yet headed all the way back to our target.”

“This is unacceptable. Higher prices drain the wallets of parents buying groceries to feed their kids and young people paying rent on their first apartments. Unpredictable increases in input costs make it more difficult for companies to plan investments and create jobs. And inflation burdens taxpayers who finance public services, schools and the national defense. We must restore price stability.”

And she argues unlike what we heard from Chair Warsh earlier this week that "[f]inancial conditions are currently providing a tailwind to the economy. Stocks, as I said, have risen notably this year. Credit spreads widened in recent weeks but remain compressed by historical standards. Banks remain eager to lend.

"Long-term interest rates have risen significantly so far in 2026, nearly a full percentage point in the case of 10-year Treasury notes. But those higher long-term rates do not represent as much of a drag on the economy as you might expect. Rates rose mainly because investors expect stronger nominal growth and higher neutral interest rates. So, the higher market rates are more a message that investors believe monetary policy has work to do than an independent headwind for activity."

"I anticipate that without any monetary policy restraint, inflation will continue to trend above target unless unexpected shocks occur. I currently estimate that the fed funds target range is at least 50 basis points—half a percentage point—below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target."

Dallas Fed President Logan (an #FOMC voter this year), who dissented in favor of a hike in July, but, a little surprisingly given her hawkish bent, went along with this week’s hold, in remarks to Davidson College students today (link below) made clear the skip changes the timing, not the destination, saying the FOMC “needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases. After that, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate."

She explains why she was fine skipping October: “Financial markets have been volatile in response to news on the technology investment outlook and geopolitical developments. In such an environment, adjusting policy more gradually can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary. Moreover, as long as market participants understand the FOMC’s policy plans, the precise timing of each rate increase has little effect on the longer-term rates most borrowers pay.”

“Indeed, by making the destination clear, the FOMC can better help the economy adapt and obtain the promised benefits of a skip.”

On inflation, she notes “While inflation has come down from the post-pandemic peak, it is not yet headed all the way back to our target.”

“This is unacceptable. Higher prices drain the wallets of parents buying groceries to feed their kids and young people paying rent on their first apartments. Unpredictable increases in input costs make it more difficult for companies to plan investments and create jobs. And inflation burdens taxpayers who finance public services, schools and the national defense. We must restore price stability.”

And she argues unlike what we heard from Chair Warsh earlier this week that "[f]inancial conditions are currently providing a tailwind to the economy. Stocks, as I said, have risen notably this year. Credit spreads widened in recent weeks but remain compressed by historical standards. Banks remain eager to lend.

"Long-term interest rates have risen significantly so far in 2026, nearly a full percentage point in the case of 10-year Treasury notes. But those higher long-term rates do not represent as much of a drag on the economy as you might expect. Rates rose mainly because investors expect stronger nominal growth and higher neutral interest rates. So, the higher market rates are more a message that investors believe monetary policy has work to do than an independent headwind for activity."

"I anticipate that without any monetary policy restraint, inflation will continue to trend above target unless unexpected shocks occur. I currently estimate that the fed funds target range is at least 50 basis points—half a percentage point—below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target."
